identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Murudeshwar Temple, on Kanduka Giri hill at the coastal town of Murudeshwar in Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka, is dedicated to Shiva worshipped here as Murudeshwara. Local tradition ties the site to the Ramayana story of the Atma Linga that the demon king Ravana obtained from Shiva and was tricked by Ganesha into setting down on the ground, after which it could not be moved; the lingam in the sanctum, set about two feet below ground level, is regarded as a remnant of that Atma Linga. The temple is not counted among the twelve Jyotirlingas. Its modern fame rests on two large twentieth/twenty-first-century additions financed by the businessman R. N. Shetty: a statue of Shiva reported at 37 metres (123 feet) and a twenty-storey entrance tower, the Raja Gopura, fitted with a lift to a viewing platform. Entry into the sanctum itself is not open to the general public.

narrative.summaryIntro: Murudeshwar Temple is a Hindu temple dedicated to Shiva, worshipped here as Murudeshwara, on Kanduka Giri hill at Murudeshwar (also spelled Murdeshwar), a coastal town in Bhatkal taluk, Uttara Kannada district, Karnataka, surrounded by the Arabian Sea on three sides. The temple is best known for two large modern structures built at the site: a statue of Shiva reported at 37 metres (123 feet), and a twenty-storey entrance tower, the Raja Gopura, fitted with a lift to an observation floor. Both were financed by the businessman and philanthropist R. N. Shetty. The temple is not one of the twelve Jyotirlingas, though Karnataka Tourism describes it as holding substantial spiritual importance in its own right, and it is one of the state's most visited pilgrimage and tourist destinations.
narrative.documentedHistory:
The temple's origin is connected in local tradition to the Ramayana story of the Atma Linga: the demon king Ravana sought the Atma-Linga from Shiva in order to gain invincibility, but Ganesha, disguised as a Brahmin boy, tricked him into setting it down on the ground at this spot, after which it could no longer be moved. Tradition holds that the cloth covering the linga was flung to "Mrideshwar" on Kanduka Giri, which is offered as the origin of the place name, and the lingam housed in the sanctum today, positioned about two feet below ground level, is regarded as a remnant of that original Atma Linga. Entry into the sanctum itself is not open to the general public; devotees performing specific sevas such as Abhisheka, Rudrabhisheka and Rathotsava are able to view the deity.

The sources consulted for this entry do not document the temple's built history before the modern period. Its present, widely recognised profile dates from a building programme financed by R. N. Shetty, credited with transforming Murudeshwar into a pilgrimage and tourist destination. The Shiva statue, built over about two years by the sculptor Kashinath of Shivamogga and others at a reported cost of approximately ₹5 crore, was completed around 2006. The twenty-storeyed Raja Gopura, fitted with a lift that gives visitors a view of the statue from an upper floor, was constructed in 2008. Two concrete elephants flank the entrance steps, and a museum called Bhukailasa Cave has been built beneath the statue.

Published claims about the statue's world ranking are inconsistent. Wikipedia's article on the temple describes it, under a flagged accuracy-dispute tag, as the "third tallest statue of Shiva in the world after Statue of Belief and Kailashnath Mahadev Statue", while Wikipedia's separate comparative list of Hindu deity statues instead calls it "the second tallest statue of Shiva in the world" and ranks it eleventh among all Hindu deity statues; Karnataka Tourism and other tourism sources likewise describe it variously as second or third tallest. This entry records only the height on which sources agree — 37 metres (123 feet) — without asserting a world ranking.

visitingInfo.dressCode: Traditional attire; trawell.in states men should wear a dhoti with shawl and women a saree or salwar kameez covering shoulders and legs, and that jeans, shorts and t-shirts are not permitted inside the temple grounds. Not corroborated by an official or government source.
visitingInfo.nearestRailStation: Murdeshwar railway station (MRDW), Konkan Railway, about 2 km from the temple
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: Sources disagree on several operational details and should be reconfirmed locally before visiting. Karnataka Tourism states temple hours as 6:00 AM–8:30 PM with morning darshan to 1:00 PM and evening darshan from 3:00 PM, while trawell.in states 3:00 AM–1:00 PM and 3:00 PM–8:00 PM. The Raja Gopura's height is given as 249 feet by Karnataka Tourism and 237 feet by trawell.in. The Uttara Kannada district government page names Bhatkal Railway Station, 18 km away, as the nearest station, whereas Wikipedia and trawell.in both describe a dedicated Murdeshwar railway station about 2 km from the temple.

shrines.locationDescription: A twenty-storeyed entrance tower built in 2008, fitted with a lift that carries visitors to an upper floor with a view of the Shiva statue. Its height is reported as 249 feet by Karnataka Tourism and as 237 feet by trawell.in; Wikipedia's temple article gives the storey count and construction year but not a height figure.

A statue of Shiva, 37 metres (123 feet) tall, on Kanduka Giri overlooking the Arabian Sea, financed by R. N. Shetty and built over about two years, completed around 2006. Sources disagree on its ranking among the world's tallest Shiva statues; see narrative for the conflicting claims.

The sanctum sanctorum, housing the main lingam positioned about two feet below ground level. Entry into the sanctum is not open to the general public; devotees performing specific sevas such as Abhisheka and Rudrabhisheka are able to view the deity.
A museum beneath the Shiva statue; its contents are not detailed in the sources consulted.

poojas.description: A special seva during which performing devotees are able to view the deity in the sanctum, which is otherwise closed to general entry.
